Learning Objectives
Specify the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors for periprosthetic fractures.
Understand what constitutes an appropriate workup for patients in whom fractures near a hip
or knee arthroplasty implant is suspected.
Apply appropriate classifications to periprosthetic fractures.
Outline surgical treatment options, including open reduction and internal fixation,
intramedullary nailing, and revision arthroplasty, based on the injury pattern and classification
and identify outcomes related to nonsurgical management.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Periprosthetic acetabulum fractures are rare, and evaluation should include assessment of the
fracture pattern, available bone stock, and implant stability.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Periprosthetic acetabulum fractures are relatively rare and underreported compared
with periprosthetic femur fractures about a total hip arthroplasty implant.1,2 A thorough
evaluation of the fracture should be performed, with a focus on the acuity of the fracture
from total hip arthroplasty, the extent of the fracture, and the components used
because management differs considerably.
Epidemiology
Periprosthetic fracture of the acetabulum is rare, with an incidence of 0.4% in press-fit
components and 0.02% in cemented cups.
Fractures occur in patients with poor bone quality during cup insertion.

Epidemiology
Periprosthetic fracture around the acetabular component is thought to be rare,
especially with use of a cemented cup. Intraoperatively, the incidence of periprosthetic
fracture with cemented and uncemented cups is 0.02%3 and 0.4%,4 respectively;
however, this maybe an underestimate1 because they are less commonly recognized. In
the postoperative period, acetabular fractures occur less frequents. Peterson and
Lewallen5 reported an incidence of 0.07% in patients with an uncemented component.
They noted that this finding led to a poor prognosis. Reports of intraoperative fractures
are shown in multiple case series and generally occur in elderly patients with poor bone
stock during cup impaction.2,6

Risk Factors
Risk factors for intraoperative fractures include use of a press-fit cup, under-reaming by 2 or
more mm, elliptical cells, poor bone quality, and need for removal of a well-fixed cup.
Postoperatively, risks include substantial osteolysis and a patient with poor bone quality
undergoing an injury.

Risk Factors
Factors associated with periprosthetic acetabulum fractures can be separated into
intraoperative and postoperative factors. The risk of an intraoperative fracture of the
acetabulum has been associated with uncemented and elliptical cups, under-reaming,
abnormal bone metabolism, and removal of a previously well-fixed acetabular
component. The risk of an intraoperative fracture in cemented components was noted
to be very rare by McElfresh and Coventry3 in 1974. Intraoperative fractures tend to
occur during impaction of a press-fit type cup into the acetabulum. In a series of 13
intraoperative fractures, all of the cups were under-reamed by 1 to 3 mm and the
fractures occurred during impaction.7 Haidukewych et al4 also noted increased risk with
the use of elliptical monoblock-type cups, reporting a prevalence of 3.5% compared with
0.09%. Abnormal bone, whether related to osteoporosis or increased sclerosis, such as
in patients with Paget disease, is associated with reported fracture.8 Revision surgery
involves the potentially difficult step of removing a well-fixed implant, which may result
in an acetabular fracture if removed with poor technique.8 Postoperative risks for
periprosthetic fractures include loss of bone integrity and traumatic injury. Traumatic
injury was implicated by Peterson and Lewallen5 in their series of 11 patients, 8 of whom
had a clear traumatic mechanism of injury. The fracture also can occur more insidiously
with no clear traumatic mechanism of injury related to osteolysis and osteopenia,
causing progressive component migration and even pelvic discontinuity.2
Injury Classification
Periprosthetic fractures about the acetabulum are classified and managed based on the
Paprosky classification of periprosthetic fractures (Figure 1).

Injury Classification
Table 1 shows the Paprosky classification of periprosthetic fractures about an
acetabular component.9 This classification system divides fractures into two general
groups—intraoperative (types I and II) and postoperative (types III, IV, and V)—because
these are the two general scenarios in which these can occur.10 Intraoperative fractures
are divided into type I and type II. Type I fractures occur during insertion of the implant;

and are subdivided based on bone stock. Type III fractures are associated with a

fractures are spontaneous fractures resulting from osteolysis and implant migration and
are subdivided based on the amount of remaining bone stock. Type V fractures are
spontaneous fractures with pelvic discontinuity and are subdivided based on bone stock
or the utility of previous radiation. The subdivisions help dictate management.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Groin pain should prompt a focused evaluation on the cup.

Patient History and Physical Examination
A traumatic injury with groin pain should prompt an evaluation of the component. The
time from total hip arthroplasty is important because a trivial mechanism of injury may
indicate a missed intraoperative fracture. Late groin pain after total hip arthroplasty may
be a sequelae of chronic osteolysis with new acute component migration.2
Imaging Studies
Radiographs are the first-line imaging study, with Judet views obtained to understand the
columns and fracture pattern.
A CT scan may aid in understanding bone quality and may be helpful for surgical planning.
A bone scan may be useful in patients with a nondisplaced, occult fracture (Figure 2).

Imaging Studies
Radiographic evaluation of a periprosthetic acetabulum fracture should begin with the
same imaging studies used in the evaluation of native acetabulum fractures. Four plain
radiographic views of the pelvis should be obtained: AP, obturator oblique (evaluation of
the anterior column), iliac oblique (evaluation of the posterior column), and false profile
views.11 This allows for evaluation of the six fundamental landmarks of the acetabulum;
however, some may be obscured by the component.12 In patients with a late fracture
related to osteolysis, radiographs may help determine the amount of bone loss and the

integrity of the columns but likely will underestimate the amount of bone loss.13 A Judet
view is particularly useful in assessing for pelvic discontinuity because fractures through
the anterior and posterior columns on a Judet view suggest pelvic discontinuity. A false
profile view is associated with a 79% sensitivity for the detection of pelvic discontinuity,
likely because of the projection of the posterior column en face.11
CT is a useful adjunct to plain radiography, especially if the diagnosis is unclear. CT has
utility in the evaluation of osteolysis and offers more precise information with regard to
volume and location of the acetabular defects.13 CT scans also are useful for evaluation
of the plane of pelvic discontinuity if present.11 CT also is performed to evaluate the
intrapelvic structures, which may potentially be at risk if medial migration is present.14
Therefore, CT has utility in the evaluation of the fracture pattern, fracture location, and
characteristics of osteolysis and in formulating a preoperative plan for safe implant
removal and subsequent reconstruction.13,14
Bone scintigraphy is a sensitive imaging modality that may be performed to aid in the
detection of fractures missed on plain radiographs or CT scans. Uptake may persist
about a total hip implant for as long as 2 years;15 however, bone scintigraphy may be
useful after the 2-year mark in patients with trauma or new groin pain who have
negative radiographs.15
Surgical Considerations
Management is dictated by the stability of the cup, the amount of bone available, and whether
the patient has received radiation, as noted by the Paprosky classification system.

Surgical Considerations
The approach to address the specific problem is determined based on the stability of the
fracture, the stability of the component, and the amount of available bone, as suggested
by the Paprosky classification system.2,9 A nondisplaced type IA fracture can be
managed via serial radiographs and protected weight-bearing.2,7 Additional screws can

nondisplaced should be managed in a manner similar to that of a type IA fracture via

Displaced fractures with adequate bone stock require surgical management to restore
the acetabular columns and cup stability (types IB, IC, IIA, IIIB, and IVA). This is most
commonly accomplished with the use of screws outside the cup, followed by screws
within the cup; with the addition of a posterior column plate; or with the use of a cup-
and-cage construct.2,4,10,16 The particular strategy will vary depending on the patient,
with fixation changing based on fracture displacement and location; reasonable
outcomes can be expected with restoration of cup integrity and alignment and fixation
of the posterior column.16 Figure 3 shows an intraoperatively recognized posterior
column fracture managed with the use of a posterior plate and screws through the cup
to restore the column and cup stability.

Pearls and Pitfalls
Appropriate identification of the fracture pattern, columns involved, bone stock, and cup
stability is crucial for selecting appropriate management.
Intraoperative fractures can be managed via cup removal, plating of the posterior column, and
augmentation of a newly inserted cup with the use of multiple screws.
Nondisplaced or minimally displaced fractures can be managed nonsurgically via protected–
weight bearing and close radiographic follow-up.
Traumatic fractures are managed based on available bone stock. If no defects are present,
anterior and posterior column plating followed by revision of the acetabular implant provides
the strongest biomechanical construct. If bone deficits are present, the surgeon should
perform cup-and-cage reconstruction or, if considerably loss is present, use a custom triflange
prosthesis.
Fractures of the Proximal Femur
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Periprosthetic femur fracture is a common reason for mortality and revision surgery after total
hip arthroplasty.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Periprosthetic femur fracture is a serious complication of total hip arthroplasty and one
of the leading causes of revision surgery.21,22 The mortality of a periprosthetic femur
fracture is 11% within 12 months of injury, which is similar to the mortality of a hip
fracture in the elderly population.23 If suspected, thoughtful evaluation and
management, ranging from simple nonsurgical management to complex revision
arthroplasty, are required.
Epidemiology
The incidence of intraoperative fracture is 1% to 7.8% and as high as 20.9% in revision surgery.
The incidence of periprosthetic fracture of the femur is 0.1% to 18%.


Epidemiology
The incidence of periprosthetic fracture may vary based on the indication for surgical
management and if the procedure is a revision procedure. In total hip arthroplasty, the
incidence of fracture ranges from 0.1% to 18%.22. Periprosthetic fracture has been
implicated as the reason for revision surgery in 16.9% of early revisions and 7.6% of late
revisions, with trauma being the most likely mechanism of injury.21 For intraoperative
fracture, the incidence ranges from 1% to 7.8% in primary total hip arthroplasty but may
be as high as 3% to 20.9% in revision total hip arthroplasty.1
Risk Factors
Risks are increased if a press-fit stem is used, if the patient has poor bone stock, during
revision surgery, and if impaction grafting is used.

Risk Factors
The risk of periprosthetic fracture appears to be increasing with time. Analysis from joint
registries has noted that revisions because of periprosthetic fractures have increased
from 2.2% in 2012 to 9.2% in 2017.23 This may be the result of multiple factors and
practices that are increasing risk, including the increase in revision surgery and the use
of noncemented implants. The rates of intraoperative fracture for noncemented
implants and cemented implants range from 1% to 7.8% and 0.3% to 1.2%, respectively.1
Omari et al24 reported that transitioning their practice to the use of cemented stems in
female patients older than 60 years reduced fracture rates within 90 days
postoperatively from 4.09% to 2.01%. Revision surgery also is associated with a
considerably higher rate of fracture.1 Fracture rate also has been evaluated based on
noncemented stem design, with increased rates occurring in tapered and fit-and-fill
designs and smaller rates in anatomic and straight-stem designs; however, data is
limited.23

Other factors have been noted to increase the risk of periprosthetic fracture. These
include female sex, inflammatory arthritis, abnormal bone in patients with metabolic
bone diseases, and non-posterior approaches.25,26 Most of these are likely because they
contribute to risks for osteolysis, osteopenia, or osteoporosis.
Finally, surgical techniques, particularly impaction grafting, have been associated with
increased fracture risk.1 The rate of fracture with impaction grafting is between 4% and
32%.1 Potential prevention of fracture may be accomplished via prophylactic cabling.27
Cortical onlay grafts also have been recommended; however, substantial evidence is
lacking.1
Injury Classification
The Vancouver classification system is the most used and helps the surgeon recommend
management.

postoperative periprosthetic fractures.1,10 The classification is shown in Table 2 and
Table 3 and illustrated in Figures 5 and 6. This classification system has been validated,

Radiographs generally are the only imaging study necessary to classify the fracture and
determine management.
A bone scan may be helpful in patients with occult fractures.

Radiographs are necessary to identify the fracture, classify the fracture appropriately,
and evaluate the stability of the implant. The fracture location should be noted on AP
and lateral radiographs of the hip to identify the specific type of fracture present.
Radiographic signs of loosening, including subsidence, change in position of the implant
compared with prior imaging studies, cement mantle fractures, and complete or
progressive radiolucencies at the bone-cement interface, should be evaluated.4
Similar to acetabular fractures, bone scintigraphy may aid in diagnosis in patients in
whom occult fractures are suspected if performed more than 2 years after
arthroplasty.15
Management
Intraoperative Fractures
Management of intraoperative periprosthetic femur fractures is based on the Vancouver
classification system and determined by the stability of the stem, the amount of available bone
stock, and the location of the fracture.

Intraoperative Fractures
Intraoperative fractures are managed according to the Vancouver classification system.
The management of cortical perforations (types A1, B1, and C1) involves bypassing the
defect, if possible, via the femoral stem, using bone graft for the defect (which can be
obtained from acetabular reamings); if extending the femoral stem is not possible, a
strut cortical graft or plate is used to augment fixation.1,29 Nondisplaced cracks in the
cortex (types A2, B2, and C2) noted postoperatively should be managed via close
observation and protected–weight bearing.1 If noted intraoperatively, they generally can
be managed with the use of cables alone after confirming that the implant is stable
(Figure 7).1,30 Finally, displaced intraoperative fractures (types A3, B3, and C3) require
management that stabilizes the femoral stem. For proximal metaphyseal fractures, a
diaphyseal-engaging stem, such as a fully porous-coated stem or a fluted tapered stem,
can be used for fixation of the fracture (Figure 8).1 For type B3 diaphyseal fractures, the

Postoperative Fractures
Management of postoperative periprosthetic fractures is based on available bone stock,
fracture location, and implant stability, as dictated by the Vancouver classification system.

Postoperative Fractures
The greatest strength of the Vancouver classification of periprosthetic proximal femur
fractures is its ability to aid in recommending appropriate management. Management

tends to be nonsurgical for type A fractures, varies based on the stability of the stem for
type B fractures, and involves fixation with the use of plates for type C fractures.
Relatively little information has been published on the management of Vancouver type A
fractures involving the lesser or greater trochanters. Most greater trochanteric fractures
are managed according to the tenets proposed by Pritchett.33 In his series, patients with
a nondisplaced or minimally displaced fracture (<2 cm) returned to acceptable function
without a limp or symptoms after physical therapy and symptom management. Patients
with more than 2 cm of displacement and persistent pain and limp were offered surgical
treatment. Fixation of the greater trochanter can be performed with the use of wires33
(Figure 9), cables,34 cable plates,35 a locking plate,36 or a locking plate and cable
construct.37,38 In general, lesser trochanteric fractures are managed nonsurgically;
however, radiographic studies should be obtained and the patient should be followed to
ensure the stem is stable.29
Similar to the type A fractures, type C fractures typically involve a stable stem and can be
managed via osteosynthesis (Figure 10). Fixation is accomplished with the use of a
locking compression plate and cables, unicortical locking screws, or bicortical nonlocking
screws around the stem if the stem overlaps the plate. If additional fixation is required,
augmentation can be accomplished with the use of an allograft strut or with the addition
of another plate to add a plane of fixation.29
Vancouver type B fractures are the most difficult to manage from a decision-making
standpoint. The classification system has developed subsets to clarify management
based on the stability of the femoral stem and the remaining bone quality. If bone

Fractures of the tibia after total knee arthroplasty are the least common fracture type

increases to almost 5% after revision surgery.

tibial tubercle osteotomy during exposure, and the insertion of a long stem.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Evaluation and management of periprosthetic patella fractures is based on the displacement

osteonecrosis.

Management
Patients with a stable component and an intact extensor mechanism are treated nonsurgically.
Patients with an intact extensor mechanism and an unstable component can be treated via
resection arthroplasty or revision of the patellar component.
Patients with a disrupted extensor mechanism require repair of the extensor mechanism or a
salvage procedure, such as mesh or allograft reconstruction.

Treatment principles for the management of periprosthetic fractures of the patella

minimally displaced and the extensor mechanism is intact, nonsurgical management in

Pearls and Pitfalls
Patellar fractures are managed nonsurgically if the implant is well fixed and the extensor
mechanism is functioning appropriately.
Patellar fractures are managed via open reduction and internal fixation or tendon
advancement if the extensor mechanism is disrupted.
In patients with a loose implant and an intact extensor mechanism, revision or removal
without revision of the component may be considered.
Salvage of a deficient extensor mechanism that cannot be fixed or advanced can be performed
with allograft augmentation or with mesh.
